title: Resolving Git Merge Conflicts: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on why Git conflicts happen, how to read markers, resolve and continue a merge or rebase, ours/theirs, mergetool, aborting, and avoiding conflicts.

chapters.title: Why Conflicts Happen
points: Definition: a conflict is Git's refusal to guess when two commits changed the same lines (or one edited a file the other deleted) since their merge base
Three-way merge: Git compares base, ours and theirs; a change on only one side is taken automatically, a different change on both sides conflicts
Common triggers: same-line edits, edit vs delete, rename vs edit, both sides adding the same file path
Conflicts can surface in merge, rebase, cherry-pick, stash pop and revert, not just merge
Mid-conflict state: git status lists 'Unmerged paths' / 'both modified', and a MERGE_HEAD (or rebase-merge dir) exists until you finish

chapters.title: Reading Conflict Markers
points: <<<<<<< HEAD down to ======= is your current side; ======= down to >>>>>>> branch is the incoming side
Resolution means editing the file to the final text and deleting all three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>)
merge.conflictStyle diff3 (or zdiff3) adds a ||||||| base section showing the original text, which makes intent much easier to judge
Choose ours, theirs, or a hand-written combination; the result must also compile and pass tests
Find leftover markers before staging: git diff --check or grep -rn '<<<<<<<' .

chapters.title: Resolve and Continue a Merge or Rebase
points: Merge workflow: git merge feature, git status, edit files, git add <file>, git commit (message pre-filled)
Rebase workflow: git rebase main, fix files, git add <file>, git rebase --continue; repeat for each conflicting commit; git rebase --skip drops the current commit
git add is what marks a file resolved; it does not need a commit in between for rebase, only --continue
List files still conflicting with git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U
Rerere: git config rerere.enabled true records your resolutions and replays them on repeated conflicts

chapters.title: Ours, Theirs and Mergetool
points: In a merge, ours = the branch you are on, theirs = the branch being merged in
In a rebase the meaning is flipped: ours = the upstream branch you are rebasing onto, theirs = your own commit being replayed
Take a whole file one way: git checkout --ours <file> or git checkout --theirs <file>, then git add
Strategy option -X ours / -X theirs only decides conflicting hunks while still merging the rest; strategy -s ours discards the other branch's changes entirely
git mergetool opens a 3-way tool (LOCAL, BASE, REMOTE, MERGED); set the tool with merge.tool, and set mergetool.keepBackup false to avoid leftover .orig files

chapters.title: Aborting and Avoiding Conflicts
points: Bail out cleanly with git merge --abort, git rebase --abort, git cherry-pick --abort; it restores the pre-operation state
Committing a file that still contains markers is the classic mistake; check with git diff --check first
Undo a bad resolution already committed: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD (merge) or git reflog to find the earlier state
Avoid conflicts: pull or rebase often, keep branches short-lived, make small focused commits, and don't reformat whole files
Agree on ownership of hot files and let a formatter or lockfile regenerate (npm install) instead of hand-merging generated files

chapters.title: Merge Conflict Cheat Sheet
points: Inspect: git status, git diff, git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U, git log --merge
Resolve: edit, git add <file>, then git commit (merge) or git rebase --continue (rebase)
Pick a side: git checkout --ours|--theirs <file>; remember the rebase flip
Escape: git merge --abort, git rebase --abort, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
Setup: merge.conflictStyle zdiff3, rerere.enabled true, merge.tool <name>, mergetool.keepBackup false
